# Purpose

This lab examines the relationships between overall workplace ratings and three workplace attitude variables: complaint handling, learning opportunities, and pay increases.

The analysis uses the built-in `attitude` dataset in R, which contains information from 30 departments. The main objective is to specify, estimate, and compare multiple linear regression models to evaluate whether these workplace attitude variables explain variation in overall workplace ratings.

The analysis follows a reproducible workflow, including data exploration, model specification, nested-model comparisons, regression diagnostics, model selection, and interpretation of regression coefficients.

# Configure the project and load packages

## Load required packages

The following packages are required for data manipulation, visualization, regression analysis, and reporting.

Install missing packages once in the R Console if necessary. Package installation is not required when rendering this document.

```{r}
# Load required packages
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(broom)
library(performance)
library(gt)
```

## Load the dataset

The built-in `attitude` dataset contains department-level summaries of employee attitudes. Each observation represents one department rather than an individual employee.

For this analysis, four numerical variables are selected:

| Variable | Description | Role |
|---|---|---|
| rating | Overall workplace rating | Outcome |
| complaints | Handling of employee complaints | Predictor |
| learning | Opportunities to learn | Predictor |
| raises | Pay increases | Predictor |

```{r}
# Load the dataset
data("attitude", package = "datasets")

# Create the analysis dataset
attitude_data <- datasets::attitude

dat <- attitude_data %>%
  select(rating, complaints, learning, raises) %>%
  drop_na()

# Number of observations
n <- nrow(dat)

# Inspect the first observations
head(dat)
```

Inspect the structure of the analysis dataset:

```{r}
str(dat)
```

The analysis dataset contains `r n` department-level observations and four numerical variables. The outcome variable is `rating`, representing overall workplace ratings. The three predictors are `complaints`, `learning`, and `raises`.

## Exploratory findings

The exploratory analysis includes 30 departments and four numerical variables.

The correlations between overall workplace ratings and the three predictors are calculated below:

The results indicate positive associations between overall workplace ratings and the three predictors. The strongest correlation can be identified using the following code:

```{r}
strongest_predictor <- names(which.max(rating_correlations))

strongest_predictor
strongest_correlation
```

The exploratory analysis included 30 departments and four numerical variables. All three predictors showed positive relationships with overall workplace rating. Complaints had the strongest correlation with rating (r = 0.825), followed by learning (r = 0.624) and raises (r = 0.590). The scatterplots generally suggested positive and approximately linear relationships. However, the degree of scatter varied across the plots. The observations in the rating-versus-raises plot appeared more closely clustered around the fitted regression line than those in the rating-versus-learning plot. Some observations in the other plots also showed considerable deviations from their respective regression lines. Overall, complaints had the strongest correlation with rating.

# Specify competing regression models

## Develop your predictions

I expect all three predictors to be positively associated with overall workplace ratings.

First, effective handling of employee complaints may contribute to a more positive workplace environment by addressing employees' concerns and improving their perceptions of organizational fairness and support. Therefore, departments with higher complaint-handling scores are expected to have higher overall workplace ratings.

Second, opportunities for learning and professional development may improve employees' skills, engagement, and job satisfaction. I expect learning to explain additional variation in overall workplace ratings beyond what is explained by complaint handling alone.

Finally, pay increases may contribute to employees' perceptions of being valued and fairly compensated. Therefore, I expect raises to potentially explain further variation in overall workplace ratings after accounting for both complaint handling and learning.

However, the additional contribution of each predictor will need to be evaluated using regression models.

## Specify four nested models

Four nested linear regression models are estimated. Each successive model includes all predictors from the preceding model.

| Model | Predictors | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| M0: Null | Intercept only | Establish a baseline |
| M1: Complaints | complaints | Evaluate complaint handling |
| M2: Complaints + Learning | complaints, learning | Evaluate the additional contribution of learning |
| M3: Expanded | complaints, learning, raises | Evaluate the additional contribution of pay increases |

```{r}
# Estimate four nested regression models

M0 <- lm(rating ~ 1, data = dat)

M1 <- lm(rating ~ complaints, data = dat)

M2 <- lm(rating ~ complaints + learning, data = dat)

M3 <- lm(rating ~ complaints + learning + raises, data = dat)
```

## Explore your fitted models

The fitted models are examined to assess the associations between the predictors and overall workplace ratings.

```{r}

# Explore your fitted models

# Store the four models in a list

models <- list(
  M0 = M0,
  M1 = M1,
  M2 = M2,
  M3 = M3
)

# Display model summaries
summary(M0)
summary(M1)
summary(M2)
summary(M3)

# Table 1: Model coefficients
coefficient_table <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  lapply(names(models), function(model_name) {
    broom::tidy(models[[model_name]]) %>%
      dplyr::mutate(Model = model_name)
  })
) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    Model, term, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value
  )

coefficient_table %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(estimate, std.error, statistic),
    decimals = 3
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = p.value,
    decimals = 4
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    Model = "Model",
    term = "Predictor",
    estimate = "Estimate",
    std.error = "Standard Error",
    statistic = "t-value",
    p.value = "P-value"
  ) %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Regression Coefficients",
    subtitle = "Coefficient estimates across the four nested models"
  )

# Table 2: Overall model performance
model_fit_table <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  lapply(names(models), function(model_name) {
    broom::glance(models[[model_name]]) %>%
      dplyr::mutate(Model = model_name)
  })
) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    Model, nobs, df.residual, r.squared,
    adj.r.squared, sigma, statistic, p.value
  )

model_fit_table %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(nobs, df.residual),
    decimals = 0
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      r.squared, adj.r.squared,
      sigma, statistic, p.value
    ),
    decimals = 4
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    Model = "Model",
    nobs = "N",
    df.residual = "Residual df",
    r.squared = "R²",
    adj.r.squared = "Adjusted R²",
    sigma = "Residual SD",
    statistic = "F-statistic",
    p.value = "Model P-value"
  ) %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Overall Model Performance",
    subtitle = "Comparison of the four nested regression models"
  )

```

The coefficient for complaints represents its association with overall workplace ratings. In Model 1, this coefficient reflects the association between complaints and ratings without adjusting for other predictors. In Model 2, it represents the association after controlling for learning opportunities. In Model 3, it represents the association after controlling for both learning opportunities and pay increases. Comparing the coefficient estimates across these models helps determine whether the association between complaint handling and overall workplace ratings changes when additional predictors are included.

# Compare model performance

This section compares the four models using nested-model F-tests, R-squared, adjusted R-squared, changes in explained variance, and RMSE.

## Conduct nested-model F-tests

The `anova()` function compares all four nested regression models in a single call, in the order M0, M1, M2, and M3.

# Compare all four nested models
```{r}
nested_anova <- anova(M0, M1, M2, M3)

nested_anova_summary <- as.data.frame(nested_anova) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(Model = c("M0", "M1", "M2", "M3")) %>%
  dplyr::select(Model, Res.Df, Df, F, `Pr(>F)`) %>%
  dplyr::rename(
    Residual_df = Res.Df,
    Change_df = Df,
    F_statistic = F,
    P_value = `Pr(>F)`
  )

nested_anova_summary

```
# Display the nested-model test results
```{r}
nested_anova_summary %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(Residual_df, Change_df),
    decimals = 0
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(F_statistic, P_value),
    decimals = 4
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    Model = "Model",
    Residual_df = "Residual df",
    Change_df = "Change in df",
    F_statistic = "F-statistic",
    P_value = "P-value"
  )
```
#The first row corresponds to the null model and does not have an incremental F-test. The remaining rows compare each model with its immediate predecessor.

#- M1 versus M0 evaluates the contribution of complaints.
#- M2 versus M1 evaluates the additional contribution of learning.
#- M3 versus M2 evaluates the additional contribution of raises.

## Extract model-level performance statistics

#The `glance()` function from the `broom` package extracts model-level statistics.

#The RMSE is calculated directly from the residuals of each fitted model.

```{r}
# Extract model-level statistics
model_performance <- bind_rows(
  glance(M0) %>% mutate(Model = "M0"),
  glance(M1) %>% mutate(Model = "M1"),
  glance(M2) %>% mutate(Model = "M2"),
  glance(M3) %>% mutate(Model = "M3")
)

# Calculate RMSE directly from model residuals
model_performance <- model_performance %>%
  mutate(
    RMSE = c(
      sqrt(mean(residuals(M0)^2)),
      sqrt(mean(residuals(M1)^2)),
      sqrt(mean(residuals(M2)^2)),
      sqrt(mean(residuals(M3)^2))
    )
  ) %>%
  select(
    Model,
    r.squared,
    adj.r.squared,
    RMSE
  )
```
# Display model performance
model_performance

# Display model performance
model_performance

R-squared represents the proportion of variation in workplace ratings explained by the model. Adjusted R-squared accounts for the number of predictors included. RMSE measures the size of residual prediction errors in the original units of workplace ratings.

## Calculate changes in explained variance

The change in R-squared (ΔR²) indicates how much additional variation is explained when a predictor is added to the preceding model.

```{r}
# Calculate changes in R-squared
model_performance <- model_performance %>%
  mutate(
    delta_R2 = r.squared - lag(r.squared)
  )

# Display the updated performance table
model_performance
```

The null model has a missing ΔR² value because there is no preceding model.

## Create a combined model-comparison table

The model-performance statistics and nested-model test results are combined using `cbind()` because both data frames contain four models in the same order.

# Combine model performance and nested-model test results

```{r}
combined_model_table <- cbind(
  model_performance,
  nested_anova_summary %>%
    dplyr::select(Residual_df, Change_df, F_statistic, P_value)
)

combined_model_table %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(Residual_df, Change_df),
    decimals = 0
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      r.squared,
      adj.r.squared,
      RMSE,
      delta_R2,
      F_statistic,
      P_value
    ),
    decimals = 4
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    Model = "Model",
    r.squared = "R²",
    adj.r.squared = "Adjusted R²",
    RMSE = "RMSE",
    delta_R2 = "ΔR²",
    Residual_df = "Residual df",
    Change_df = "Change in df",
    F_statistic = "Nested F",
    P_value = "Nested p"
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Overall Model Performance",
    columns = c(r.squared, adj.r.squared, RMSE)
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Incremental Model Improvement",
    columns = c(delta_R2, Residual_df, Change_df, F_statistic, P_value)
  ) %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Comparison of the Four Nested Regression Models",
    subtitle = "Model fit and incremental improvements"
  )
```
## Interpret the comparisons

#The following values are extracted directly from the combined comparison table.

```{r}
# Identify the model with the highest R-squared
best_R2_model <- model_performance %>%
  dplyr::slice_max(r.squared, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

best_R2_value <- best_R2_model$r.squared

# Calculate the R-squared improvement for M1
# Calculate R-squared improvements for each model
m1_delta <- model_performance$delta_R2[
  model_performance$Model == "M1"
]

m2_delta <- model_performance$delta_R2[
  model_performance$Model == "M2"
]

m3_delta <- model_performance$delta_R2[
  model_performance$Model == "M3"
]

# Identify the model with the highest adjusted R-squared
best_adjusted_model <- model_performance %>%
  dplyr::slice_max(adj.r.squared, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

# Display the key results
best_R2_model %>%
  dplyr::select(Model, r.squared, adj.r.squared, RMSE)

best_adjusted_model %>%
  dplyr::select(Model, r.squared, adj.r.squared, RMSE)

# Display incremental improvements
combined_model_table %>%
  dplyr::select(Model, delta_R2, F_statistic, P_value, RMSE)
```

1. Which model explains the largest proportion of variation in rating?

Model M3 explains the largest proportion of variation in rating, with an R² of 0.7083 (70.83%). However, its improvement over M2 is extremely small, suggesting that adding raises contributes very little additional explanatory power.

2. How does adjusted R² change as predictors are added?

Adjusted R² increases from 0.6699 in M1 to 0.6864 in M2, indicating a modest improvement after adding learning. However, it decreases to 0.6746 in M3, suggesting that adding raises does not justify the increased model complexity.

3. How much additional variation does each successive model explain?
- M0 to M1: R² increases by 68.13 percentage points.
- M1 to M2: R² increases by 2.67 percentage points.
- M2 to M3: R² increases by only 0.03 percentage points.
These results indicate that complaints accounts for most of the explained variation, while learning provides a relatively small additional contribution and raises contributes almost nothing.

4. Which additions produce statistically significant improvements in fit?

Adding complaints in M1 significantly improves model fit (p = 1.988 × 10⁻⁸). However, adding learning in M2 does not produce a statistically significant improvement (p = 0.128), and adding raises in M3 also fails to significantly improve model fit (p = 0.876).

5. Do the reductions in RMSE appear substantively meaningful?

RMSE decreases from 12.17 in M0 to 6.99 in M1, representing a substantial improvement in model fit. However, the reduction from 6.99 to 6.82 in M2 is relatively small, while RMSE increases slightly to 6.94 in M3. Therefore, most of the improvement in predictive accuracy occurs when complaints is added.

Overall conclusion:
Overall, complaints is the strongest contributor to explaining variation in rating. Although adding learning produces a small increase in R², this improvement is not statistically significant. Adding raises provides virtually no additional explanatory value. Therefore, M1 may be preferred as a more parsimonious model, despite M3 having the highest numerical R².

# Evaluate regression diagnostics

## Select a candidate model for diagnostic evaluation

The model with the highest adjusted R-squared among M1, M2, and M3 is selected as the initial candidate.

This is a provisional choice. The diagnostic results and substantive interpretability must also be considered before finalizing the preferred model.

```{r}
candidate_name <- model_performance %>%
  filter(Model != "M0") %>%
  slice_max(
    adj.r.squared,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) %>%
  pull(Model)

candidate_model <- switch(
  candidate_name,
  "M1" = M1,
  "M2" = M2,
  "M3" = M3
)

candidate_name

summary(candidate_model)
```

## Examine the regression assumptions

Standard regression diagnostic plots are used to examine linearity, residual normality, homoscedasticity, and potentially influential observations.

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(candidate_model)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

performance::check_model(candidate_model)
```

The `check_model()` function provides an additional visual assessment of the regression assumptions.

```{r}
performance::check_collinearity(candidate_model)
```

## Examine multicollinearity

Multicollinearity can make it difficult to estimate the unique contribution of individual predictors.

```{r}
if (length(coef(candidate_model)) > 2) {

  performance::check_collinearity(candidate_model)

} else {

  cat(
    "The candidate model contains only one predictor. ",
    "Multicollinearity among multiple predictors is not applicable."
  )

}
```

## Report your diagnostic findings

### Diagnostic Findings

Diagnostic plots for the selected model (M2), which included complaints and learning as predictors, indicated that the linearity assumption was reasonably satisfied, with no strong systematic pattern in the residuals. However, minor deviations from normality were observed at the tails of the Q-Q plot, and the Scale-Location plot suggested some variation in residual spread, indicating possible mild heteroscedasticity. Although observation 24 showed relatively high leverage, it did not appear to be strongly influential based on Cook's distance. Furthermore, multicollinearity was not a major concern, as the VIF values for both predictors were below 5. The observed and model-predicted distributions were also reasonably similar. Overall, these findings suggest that the model is reasonably appropriate, although the potential deviations from normality and constant variance warrant some caution when interpreting the results. These limitations do not invalidate the model, but they suggest that the estimated relationships should be interpreted cautiously.

# Select and report your preferred model

## Select a model

The candidate model is initially selected based on adjusted R-squared. The final decision should also consider the nested-model F-tests, changes in R-squared, RMSE, model complexity, diagnostic findings, and substantive interpretability.

The following object identifies the preferred model. If your diagnostic assessment supports a different model, change `preferred_model_name` to `"M1"`, `"M2"`, or `"M3"` before rendering the report.

```{r}
# Select M1 as the preferred model

preferred_model_name <- "M1"

preferred_model <- switch(
  preferred_model_name,
  "M1" = M1,
  "M2" = M2,
  "M3" = M3
)

preferred_model_name

summary(preferred_model)
```

The preferred model is `r preferred_model_name`. This model was initially selected because it has the highest adjusted R-squared among the three predictor models.

However, the final choice should also reflect whether the additional predictors provide statistically significant improvements, whether RMSE decreases meaningfully, and whether the diagnostic plots indicate serious violations of regression assumptions.

A more complex model is not necessarily preferable if the additional predictors provide little improvement in model fit or make the interpretation less precise.

## Create a coefficient table

The `tidy()` function from the `broom` package is used to extract the estimated regression coefficients and their 95% confidence intervals.

```{r}
selected_tidy <- broom::tidy(
  preferred_model,
  conf.int = TRUE,
  conf.level = 0.95
)

coefficient_table <- selected_tidy %>%
  dplyr::select(
    Predictor = term,
    Estimate = estimate,
    Standard_Error = std.error,
    CI_Lower = conf.low,
    CI_Upper = conf.high,
    p_value = p.value
  )

coefficient_table %>%
  gt::gt() %>%
  gt::fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      Estimate,
      Standard_Error,
      CI_Lower,
      CI_Upper
    ),
    decimals = 3
  ) %>%
  gt::fmt_number(
    columns = p_value,
    decimals = 4
  ) %>%
  gt::cols_label(
    Predictor = "Predictor",
    Estimate = "Coefficient",
    Standard_Error = "Standard Error",
    CI_Lower = "95% CI Lower",
    CI_Upper = "95% CI Upper",
    p_value = "p-value"
  ) %>%
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "Regression Coefficients",
    subtitle = paste(
      "Preferred model:",
      preferred_model_name
    )
  )
```

## Interpret the coefficients
```{r}
interpret_coefficient <- function(variable) {

  result <- selected_tidy %>%
    dplyr::filter(term == variable)

  if (nrow(result) == 0) {
    return(NULL)
  }

  estimate <- result %>%
    dplyr::pull(estimate)

  lower <- result %>%
    dplyr::pull(conf.low)

  upper <- result %>%
    dplyr::pull(conf.high)

  direction <- if (estimate > 0) {
    "positive"
  } else if (estimate < 0) {
    "negative"
  } else {
    "approximately zero"
  }

  paste0(
    "For ", variable,
    ", the estimated coefficient is ",
    round(estimate, 3),
    ", indicating a ", direction,
    " association with overall ratings. ",
    "A one-unit increase in complaints is associated with an estimated ",
    round(estimate, 3),
    " point increase in overall ratings. ",
    "Since M1 includes only one predictor, no other predictors are held constant. ",
    "The 95% confidence interval ranges from ",
    round(lower, 3),
    " to ",
    round(upper, 3),
    "."
  )
}

coefficient_interpretations <- c(
  interpret_coefficient("complaints")
)

cat(
  paste(
    coefficient_interpretations,
    collapse = "\n\n"
  )
)
```

1. Direction of the association

The regression coefficient for complaints was positive, indicating a positive association between complaints and overall ratings. This suggests that departments with higher complaint scores tended to have higher overall rating scores.

2. Interpretation of the coefficient in the original units

For every one-unit increase in the complaints score, the predicted overall rating increased by approximately r round(complaints_result, 3) points. Both variables are measured in their original score units.

3. Variables held constant

Since M1 includes complaints as the only predictor, no other explanatory variables were held constant. Therefore, the coefficient represents the unadjusted association between complaints and overall ratings.

4. Uncertainty reflected in the confidence interval

The 95% confidence interval for the complaints coefficient ranged from r round(complaints_lower, 3) to r round(complaints_upper, 3). Since the entire interval is above zero, the results support a positive association between complaints and overall ratings. The confidence interval also indicates the uncertainty surrounding the estimated regression coefficient.

## Summarize model performance

The following values are extracted from the selected model.
```{r}
selected_performance <- model_performance %>%
  dplyr::filter(Model == preferred_model_name)

selected_r2 <- selected_performance %>%
  dplyr::pull(r.squared)

selected_adjusted_r2 <- selected_performance %>%
  dplyr::pull(adj.r.squared)

selected_rmse <- selected_performance %>%
  dplyr::pull(RMSE)
```
```{r}
model_R2 <- summary(preferred_model)$r.squared

model_adjusted_R2 <- summary(preferred_model)$adj.r.squared

model_RMSE <- sqrt(mean(residuals(preferred_model)^2))
```

The preferred model (M1) had an R-squared (R²) of r round(selected_r2, 3), indicating that complaints explained approximately r round(selected_r2 * 100, 1)% of the variation in overall workplace ratings across departments.

Its adjusted R-squared was r round(selected_adjusted_r2, 3), which accounts for the number of predictors included in the model. This indicates that the model retained a similar level of explanatory power after accounting for model complexity.

The root mean square error (RMSE) was r round(selected_rmse, 3) points, representing the typical magnitude of prediction errors in the original units of overall workplace ratings. A lower RMSE indicates that the model's predicted ratings are closer to the observed ratings.

Overall, these statistics suggest that M1 provides a reasonable level of explanatory and predictive performance while maintaining a relatively simple structure with only one predictor.

# Discuss findings and limitations

The analysis examines the relative contributions of complaint handling, learning opportunities, and pay increases to overall workplace ratings.

1. Complaint Handling

Complaint handling appeared to be the most important predictor of overall workplace ratings among the three variables examined. In Model M1, complaints explained approximately 68.13% of the variation in overall ratings (R² = 0.6813). The association was positive and statistically significant (p < 0.001), suggesting that departments with higher complaint-handling scores tended to have higher overall workplace ratings. Furthermore, complaints remained a statistically significant predictor when learning opportunities and pay increases were added to the model.

2. Learning Opportunities

Learning opportunities provided a relatively small additional contribution to explaining overall workplace ratings. When learning was added to M1 to create M2, R² increased from 0.6813 to 0.7080, representing an increase of approximately 2.67 percentage points. However, this improvement was not statistically significant (p = 0.128). This suggests that learning opportunities did not provide sufficient additional explanatory value beyond complaint handling in this dataset.

3. Pay Increases

Pay increases contributed very little additional explanatory power. When raises were added to M2 to create M3, R² increased by only approximately 0.03 percentage points. This improvement was not statistically significant (p = 0.876). Therefore, raises did not meaningfully improve the explanatory performance of the model after accounting for complaints and learning.

4. Overall Comparison

Overall, complaint handling demonstrated the strongest statistical association with workplace ratings among the three predictors. Learning opportunities showed a modest additional contribution, whereas pay increases provided almost no additional explanatory value in the models examined. These findings support selecting M1 as the preferred model because it captures most of the explanatory information while maintaining a simpler structure.
